name: The Pygmalion Effect
statement: Higher expectations of a person tend to raise their performance.
meaning: When someone in authority — a teacher, a manager, an officer — believes a person will do well, that person tends to do better, not because they were truly more capable, but because the belief changes how they are treated, which changes the outcome. The expectation helps make itself come true.
mechanism: It is a specific self-fulfilling prophecy. An expectation changes behaviour toward the person — more warmth, more challenging material, more chances to respond, more feedback — and that changed treatment, internalised as higher self-expectation and backed by more support, improves the outcome, which then confirms the original belief. Rosenthal summarised the pathway as four factors: a warmer climate, more input, more response opportunity, and more feedback.

examples.text: In Rosenthal and Jacobson's 1968 study, teachers were told a randomly chosen fifth of pupils were 'intellectual bloomers' poised to spurt, identified by a fictitious test. Those randomly labelled children then showed larger gains on later IQ testing — attributed to subtly different teacher treatment, not real difference.

J. Sterling Livingston's 1969 Harvard Business Review essay 'Pygmalion in Management' argued a manager's expectations shape a subordinate's performance: high expectations tend to lift it, low expectations to depress it — the workplace form of the self-fulfilling prophecy.

Eden and Shani (1982) told instructors on a military command course that certain randomly designated trainees had high 'command potential'. Those trainees went on to score higher on objective tests and leadership — evidence the effect extends beyond the classroom.

variants.name: The golem effect
variants.text: The negative counterpart: low expectations lead to decreased performance, the same self-fulfilling machinery running downhill.

variants.name: The self-fulfilling prophecy
variants.text: The general concept the Pygmalion effect is a case of — a belief that brings about its own fulfilment, a term coined by the sociologist Robert K. Merton in 1948.

variants.name: The Galatea effect
variants.text: Performance driven by a person's own self-expectations and self-efficacy rather than someone else's expectations — named for the statue Pygmalion carved, and studied by Eden and colleagues.

whyItMatters: It made vivid the idea that expectations are not passive predictions but active forces that shape the outcomes they anticipate — a lesson that reshaped thinking about teaching, management, and bias. It is also a standing warning that low expectations can quietly become self-confirming, entrenching the very gaps they assume.

working.text: since expectations shape treatment and treatment shapes outcomes, expecting more of people — and showing it through warmth, challenge, and feedback — can genuinely help.
watch for low expectations of individuals or groups becoming self-fulfilling; the same mechanism that lifts can also entrench disadvantage.
the effect is real but modest and context-dependent; treat it as one lever among many, not a guarantee that belief alone transforms performance.

limits: The founding 1968 study was seriously criticised. Robert L. Thorndike attacked the IQ instrument, showing baseline scores were implausible — one class's average reasoning IQ fell in the range then called mentally disabled, which he argued was impossible and rendered the measure meaningless — and concluded the findings were essentially worthless. Effect sizes are modest and highly context-dependent: expectancy effects are much stronger when induced before teachers know their students, and Raudenbush's meta-analysis found the induced effect fell to roughly zero once teachers had known students a couple of weeks. Meta-analyses support a genuine but small effect; the popular claim that expectations powerfully determine outcomes is not well supported.
misreadings: It is not proof that belief alone can transform anyone, and the original IQ result should never be cited without its critique. The effect is real in aggregate but modest and easy to overstate — strongest before an evaluator forms independent impressions, and weak or absent once they know the person. The famous classroom study is a flawed demonstration, not a clean one.
origin: From Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson's 1968 book Pygmalion in the Classroom, reporting that randomly labelled 'bloomers' outperformed peers after teachers were led to expect it. Named for Pygmalion, the sculptor of Greek myth whose statue came to life; the workplace form was popularised by J. Sterling Livingston's 1969 Harvard Business Review essay. The founding study drew a sharp methodological critique from Robert L. Thorndike.

sources.text: Rosenthal, R. & Jacobson, L. (1968). Pygmalion in the Classroom: Teacher Expectation and Pupils' Intellectual Development. Holt, Rinehart & Winston.
